It's been a while since we last connected on how the Social Science Data Archive's
successor is doing. Here's a short update on what DSC has built since then, with an eye
toward the parts that touch the social sciences directly.

::: {.tldr}
**In short:** Dataverse has grown from 9 datasets in 2020 to over 1,600 today. DSC's
Redivis platform, built around an unusable 10-terabyte national voter file, has since
processed 4.8 petabytes of restricted research data. About 1 in 8 workshop attendees
since 2020 have come from social science departments. And GIS support disappeared in
2024, even though the demand for it never did.
:::

These check-ins were a regular practice in the Archive's early years at the Library.
This update is an attempt to pick that back up. One person bridges nearly the whole
modern era: **Jamie Jamison**, who transferred with the Archive in 2014, is still on
the DSC team today.

## Social sciences remain a core constituency

[About 1 in 8 workshop attendees since 2020 came from social science departments.]{.lede}

Workshop attendance since 2020 includes roughly **200 participants**, about 1 in 8 of
all UCLA attendees, from social science and social-science-adjacent departments:
Geography, Psychology, Political Science, Sociology, Economics, Anthropology, Urban
Planning, Public Policy, and Gender Studies, plus people who registered simply as
"Social Science." The Archive's original subscriptions from the 2014 transfer,
including ICPSR (~$47K/year) and the Roper Center (~$8K/year), are still funded
through the Archive's original gift fund (FAU 605000-DA-56972), the same fund that
came over with the transfer.

## Redivis and the L2 voter file

[DSC turned an unusable 10-terabyte national voter file into a resource social scientists across campus now use directly.]{.lede}

DSC piloted **Redivis**, a secure platform for restricted research data, initially
supported by University Librarian discretionary funds. It's since grown into a
sustained subscription, about $47K/year as of 2026, paid through Library central
finance alongside ICPSR and Roper. The platform holds about 20TB of P3/P4-compliant
data (FERPA, PII, HIPAA) across 50 registered users and over 150 workflows, and has
processed **4.8 petabytes** cumulatively since it launched in 2022.

The flagship dataset is the **L2 historic voter file**, over 10TB of national voter
history purchased by DSC and a Library subject selector through the same gift fund
that covers ICPSR and Roper. It arrived as thousands of fragmented, state-level files,
too large to store locally and too inconsistent to analyze as-is. DSC consolidated it
into a single, version-controlled, analysis-ready dataset, cited by Redivis's own CEO
as a flagship use case at FORCE11 2024.

Researchers are using it directly: gentrification patterns in Inglewood, election
administration, Latino voting behavior, and a project merging the voter file with UCLA
medical records to study health and voting, led by faculty across Political Science,
Economics, and Health. As the graduate student who curated the dataset put it:

> *"Professors and students in a social sciences department are able to instantly work with a large, rich dataset in a secure environment."*
> — Graham Straus, UCLA Political Science PhD student, FORCE11 2024

## GIS and geospatial support

[UCLA cut its GIS librarian position in 2024. Demand didn't go with it.]{.lede}

Geography has consistently been DSC's single largest workshop constituency: 64 of the
roughly 1,575 UCLA workshop attendees since 2020, more than any other department.

Before the position was eliminated in 2024, DSC's GIS librarian handled 72 to 82
booked consultations a year (2021 to 2023) across Urban Planning, Public Affairs,
Environment and Sustainability, and Digital Humanities. They also co-taught a graduate
Public Health course, ran systemwide UC GIS workshops that reached 617 participants in
2023 alone, and managed key research datasets, including the LARIAC aerial imagery
acquired through the Archive's gift fund. That demand hasn't gone away. DSC still
fields GIS requests, just without the specialist capacity to meet them.

Nationally, 81 of 187 Carnegie R1 institutions (43%) maintain a dedicated GIS
librarian, rising to 81% among the top 25 R&D-spending universities. UCLA has the
highest research expenditure of any UC campus, yet is one of only two UC R1 campuses
without one. The other, Santa Cruz, spends a fraction of what UCLA does on research.
(UCSF also lacks one, but it's a health-sciences-only campus with no undergraduates,
not a fair comparison; most medical centers don't staff GIS librarians.) Lower-spending
UC peers like Berkeley and San Diego both maintain dedicated GIS staff.

Campus-wide, UCLA's ArcGIS Online platform, used across Geography, Luskin, Fielding,
Digital Humanities, Political Science, and Social Data Science, has over 7,100
accounts and more than 3,000 active users in the past year, per an OARC governance
report from December 2025. Without a designated administrator, it's now running at
over 200% of its licensed storage.

## Consulting spotlights

::: {.spotlight}
### Carceral Ecologies
[Partner: UCLA Institute for Society and Genetics (Nicholas Shapiro)]{.partners}

DSC and DataSquad provided multi-year research support, including R server
infrastructure, data processing, and training for a research student who later joined
the lab as staff, for work on a massive helicopter surveillance dataset that outstripped
the lab's ability to host locally. That work became the pilot study behind a $5 million
grant that established the Dana Center for Neuroscience and Society.

> *"This work wouldn't have happened without your team!"*
> — Dr. Nicholas Shapiro, UCLA Institute for Society and Genetics

[**Outcome:** processing time cut from ~318 minutes to ~2 minutes (~159x faster), with a research student trained in the resulting R workflow. **Impact:** coverage in the *Los Angeles Times*, *The New Yorker*, and *Bloomberg*.]{.impact}
:::

::: {.spotlight}
### BioCritical Studies Lab
[Partner: UCLA (Grace Sosa; Terence Keel)]{.partners}

A multi-year collaboration (2021 to 2024) on data integration, statistical analysis,
and visualization for a comprehensive U.S. deaths-in-custody dataset, with tools built
for the lab to maintain independently. The dataset has supported projects funded by
NIH, NSF, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, and Prof. Keel's resulting book is
now published.

> *"It is one of the most impactful resources I have engaged with [...] at UCLA."*
> — Grace Sosa, Assistant Director, BioCritical Studies Lab

[**Impact:** supported research recognized through UCLA's 2024 Public Impact Research Awards, contributing to public-facing scholarship and teaching.]{.impact}
:::

## DataSquad

[DataSquad's project work grew from 6 tasks in 2023 to 111 in 2025.]{.lede}

DataSquad is DSC's peer-consulting model: undergraduate and graduate student
consultants providing sustained project support alongside DSC staff's direct
consultations. Reportable project work grew from **6 tasks in 2023 to 111 in 2025**,
as demand shifted from one-off consultations toward sustained, hands-on project
support.

The program started in 2020 on a gift from **Norman Powell**, which funded student
salaries and laptops for the first cohort. The Library added funding in 2023 to
expand the team and add in-person hours. In 2024, DataSquad absorbed the LuxLab
student program after its funding source, CLICC funds, became restricted, merging two
student-support lines into one.

## Infrastructure

[Dataverse has grown from 9 datasets in 2020 to 1,603 today.]{.lede}

Dataverse, UCLA's institutional repository, which DSC operates, has grown from 9
datasets and 229 downloads in January 2020 to **1,603 datasets and over 143,000
downloads** today. This is the same hosting commitment the Library made in the 2014
transfer ("necessary technological infrastructure for continued hosting of software,
data, and data analysis tools"), grown considerably since.

Dataverse, Redivis, and the Archive's core subscriptions (ICPSR, Roper) are funded
through a mix of the Library's central budget, University Librarian discretionary
funds, and the original SSDA gift fund, the same combination of sources that has
supported most of DSC's growth.
